questions: what is the museum of ordinary life
what is museum of ordinary life
what kind of museum is this
why is there a museum of ordinary life
answer: The Museum of Ordinary Life is an archive established in 2026. It documents ordinary objects, rooms, interfaces, routines, paperwork, sounds, stories, and the context around them while that context can still be recorded. For now, it’s a distributed digital archive rather than a single building.

questions: what is the point of this museum
why should anyone care about ordinary life
answer: Much of ordinary life disappears without leaving much of a record. Bedrooms, receipts, routines, interfaces, clutter, workarounds, waiting, maintenance, and small habits are easy to lose. The Museum records them before we know which details people will later wish somebody had saved. A life doesn’t have to be exceptional to matter.

questions: why does the collection start in 2026
answer: Because 2026 is when the Museum started. The collection begins in the present instead of trying to reconstruct ordinary context after it has already disappeared.

questions: what can go in the museum
what kinds of things do you collect
can anything be in the museum
what kind of stuff do you want
would this belong in the museum
answer: Almost anything can count if it helps explain how everyday life worked. The Museum is interested in the thing and its context: what it was, where it lived, how it was used, who used it, and when. Rarity, beauty, and a profound story aren’t requirements.

questions: what sections are in the collection
give me examples of what you collect
answer: The current collection categories are Home, Work, Money, Technology, Public life, Paperwork, Routine, and Digital traces. They’re starting points, not strict boxes.

questions: how do i document ordinary life
how do i take a museum photo
how should i photograph an object
how much context should i include
answer: Keep the thing and its surroundings together. One useful method is to photograph an object twice: once clearly, then again where it normally lives. Save interfaces before they disappear. Don’t worry about making the record profound. A fragment can be useful without explaining a whole person.

where do i send a contribution
how to add something to the museum
okay how do i send something
how can i give the museum something
what do i do if i want to contribute
answer: Send the original photo, video, audio file, screenshot, or document when possible. Tell us what it is and when you documented it. Add an approximate location if it matters and whatever context you want preserved. Then choose publication and reuse permissions separately.

questions: what file types can i send
what kind of files do you accept
can i send you a picture
answer: The site currently asks for original photos, videos, audio files, screenshots, or documents when possible. If what you want to preserve doesn’t fit those forms, contact the Museum rather than forcing it into the wrong format.

questions: why do you want the original file
should i send the original photo
can i send an edited image
can i send a resized image
should i edit my photo first
answer: The Museum prefers the original file or record when possible because it preserves more of the record. Public copies may later be cropped, resized, or redacted while the archival original is kept separately.

questions: what do i say about my contribution
when should i say it was made
answer: At minimum, say what the thing or record is and when you documented it. The Museum also asks for an approximate location when it matters and any context you want to keep with the record.

questions: do i need to give my location
do i have to say where it is
answer: Give an approximate location only if it matters to the record. A city name is plenty. The contribution instructions do not ask for a precise street address.

questions: how much context do i need
do i need to explain it
what should i write about it
answer: Add as much or as little context as feels right. One sentence can be enough. No explanation can also be useful information. Context might include where something lived, how it was used, what surrounded it, or what it meant to you.

questions: can i choose whether it is public
answer: Submitting something to the archive doesn’t automatically make it public. Preservation and publication are separate. You can allow public display now, choose a later release, ask the Museum to check with you again, or preserve the record without public display.

questions: do i have to use my name
can i contribute without my name
answer: Yes. The current permission model allows public display with your name or anonymously. Attribution for other permitted uses is also recorded separately.

questions: can you publish it in ten years
can i choose a release date
can i keep it closed for years
answer: You can choose a delayed release. The current options include publication on or after a chosen date, waiting a chosen number of years, asking again later, or keeping the record archive-only.

questions: can you preserve it but not publish it
can i submit something that never goes public
can it stay private in the archive
answer: Yes. A contribution can be preserved without public display. The current contribution choices include “archive only and ask before publishing” and “archive only; don’t publish.” Archive-only status doesn’t automatically grant research, machine learning, or generative-reuse permission.
